passage.title: Text A: We Are Treating the Sea as a Bin
passage.byline: A modern article by a marine conservation diver
paras: Last summer, on a beach in Cornwall, I picked up a crisp packet. The best-before date printed on it was older than I am. It had been drifting for decades, faded but whole, and it will still be drifting long after I am gone.

We all know the pictures by now: the turtle tangled in netting, the seabird whose stomach is full of bottle tops. We share them, we sigh, and then we buy our lunch wrapped in three layers of plastic. One widely quoted estimate says that a rubbish lorry's worth of plastic enters the sea every minute. Even if the true figure were half that, it would be a disgrace.

The problem is not that plastic exists. It is that we use it for seconds and throw it into a system that keeps it for centuries. Rivers carry it to the coast; tides break it into fragments so small that fish mistake them for food; and those fish end up on our plates. The sea is handing our rubbish back to us, one meal at a time.

Some say that the ocean is too vast to harm, that one bottle cannot matter. But the ocean is not a bottomless pit. It is a living system, and we are part of it. Fishing communities already report smaller catches; reefs that once glowed with colour are turning grey.
There are answers. Refill schemes, deposit returns on bottles and bans on single-use bags have all cut litter where they have been tried. None of them needs a miracle, only the will to start.

I have dived in waters so clear you could read a newspaper on the seabed, and I have dived in waters choked with bags that drift like ghosts. We are not short of evidence; we are short of courage. If we keep treating the sea as a bin, we should not be surprised when it stops feeding us.
